rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king admired Joseph because his dream interpretation satisfied everyone and Joseph also proposed a plan to counter the drought foretold by the dream.
rows.anchor: Such was this interpretation that it satisfied everyone. Then what further impressed him was that Joseph (sws) explained a scheme to combat this horrible drought

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's refusal to leave prison until the charges were investigated, followed by his complete exoneration, further impressed the king.
rows.anchor: he did not accept it until the allegations upon him that sent him to prison were investigated, he was totally absolved from them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because monarchy concentrates power in the king, naming Joseph his trusted assistant effectively announced that the king would entrust his powers to him along with releasing him.
rows.anchor: In monarchies, all powers are concntrated in the person of the king. So, if he makes someone his trusted assistant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king and Joseph had not previously spoken directly; others mediated, but their meeting likely covered religious, moral, administrative, and economic matters and increased the king's admiration.
rows.anchor: Until then, there had not been any direct exchange between the two; some individuals were mediating between them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king offered Joseph virtually the reins of government and left the extent of his acceptance to Joseph's discretion.
rows.anchor: he offered to virtually consign the reins of his government to him, and left the extent of its acceptance to the discretion of Joseph (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here, 'the land' means Egypt, and its treasures are the country's means of production.
rows.anchor: means of production of the country.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's request was a practical proposal to implement the king's offer, not a request for appointment; he declared his competence and expected to do the work well.
rows.anchor: It should remain clear that this was not a request from Joseph (sws). It was a practical suggestion from him to implement the offer made to him by the king

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's proposal met the king's desire, effectively transferring control of the country to Joseph; Genesis likewise describes Pharaoh placing him in charge of Egypt.
rows.anchor: In this way, the reins of the country were virtually handed over to Joseph (sws). In the book of Genesis, it is stated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression means Joseph could reside and travel anywhere in the kingdom, govern as he chose, and issue orders that officials had to obey.
rows.anchor: Joseph (sws) could stay anyehere in the kingdom and visit whichever part of the kingdom he wantes to; he could run the empire any way he wanted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone holds sovereignty and can raise even a prisoner to rule; no one can prevent His choice to grant grace.
rows.anchor: all sovereignty belongs to God. If He wants to bless someone with His grace, none can stop Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thorough face trials, and steadfastness brings them reward from God in this world and the next.
rows.anchor: The thorough are richly rewarded for their deeds. They do face trials. If they remain steadfast in facing them, they are rewarded by God in this world as well as in the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers arrived seven years later during drought across Egypt, Syria, and Palestine; Joseph's prior measures left Egypt self-sufficient and supplying neighboring countries through rationed grain sales.
rows.anchor: This happened seven years after when not only Egypt but also its neighbouring countries like Syria and Palestine had been engulfed by drought

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As foreigners, the brothers seem to have needed Joseph's special permission to buy grain.
rows.anchor: since his brothers belonged to a different country, they had to seek special permission from Joseph (sws) to acquire grain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers failed to recognize Joseph after more than two decades because his appearance had changed; even a resemblance could not suggest that the brother they cast in a well had become Egypt's king.
rows.anchor: they had not seen him for more than two decades after casting him into the well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grain was rationed according to household size, so Joseph asked the brothers to disclose their stepbrother and bring him next time, urging them with full measure and hospitality and threatening to refuse future grain otherwise.
rows.anchor: a rationing system to give grain was in place in the country. The needy were given this grain in accordance with the number of people in a family

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kīl literally means a vessel of known capacity; here it refers to the grain it contains, naming the content through its container.
rows.anchor: The word !ۡﻛﻴﻞ actually means a utensil with a known capacity. Here it means the grain a utensil holds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb yamm means to provide grain and other necessities to one's family.
rows.anchor: to provide grain and other things of need to one’s family

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers imply that failure to bring Benjamin would be their father's doing, revealing their lingering guilt over what they did to Joseph.
rows.anchor: Concealed in this sentence was their purport that if they were not able to bring their brother, it would not be their fault

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph returned the brothers' currency to encourage them to come back.
rows.anchor: Joseph (sws) did this to induce them to come again

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's words show his trust in the brothers had been broken; if he sent Benjamin, he would entrust him to God for protection.
rows.anchor: his trust had on them had been broken and if he had to send Benjamin along with them, he would do it by trusting God and giving him in His protection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's eloquence conveys the brothers' jubilation by suppressing a coordinated clause, which the translator supplies.
rows.anchor: The co-ordinated sentence of !!ﻠﻨﺎۡﻫ has been suppressed here and I have revealed it in the translation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One camel-load per person was allowed to foreign visitors under Joseph's rationing system.
rows.anchor: as per the rationing system implemented by Joseph (sws), visitors from abroad had the permission of acquiring one camel-load of grain per person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse recounts Jacob's proposal about sending Benjamin.
rows.anchor: Jacob’s proposition in sending Benjamin is referred to here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression means that Jacob's advice could not benefit the sons in the slightest against God's will.
rows.anchor: The expression   #ۡﻜﻢ!ۡﻋﻨ ۡ ۡﻏ means “it cannot be of slightest benefit to you.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob advised them to enter separately because drought increases theft and robbery, and eleven graceful, attractive men entering together might draw attention and be attacked or robbed by city rogues.
rows.anchor: in times of a drought, the chance of theft and robbery and other similar crimes increase a lot

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's practical advice was not meant to suggest that precautions could override God's certain will.
rows.anchor: This advice from him must never be construed by his sons that it could override the will of God, which is certain to be implemented

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although people must strive, the outcome depends on God's will; no one can change His decision.
rows.anchor: No one can change His decision.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse praises Jacob for learning from God to distinguish planning from ordained fate.
rows.anchor: he knew how to distinguish between planning and the ordained fate for that planning; this knowledge was taught to him by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People commonly either treat planning as everything and disregard fate, or invoke fate to excuse making no effort.
rows.anchor: Either they regard planning to be everything and disregard fate or in the name of accepting whatever fate comes their way do not even strive and make effort.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph privately identified himself to Benjamin and, the surrounding indications suggest, explained the plan so Benjamin would be reassured.
rows.anchor: Concomitant indications show that at that time he must have also made him aware of the plan he had in mind for keeping him so that he remain assured

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The royal cup was a scale used to measure grain and Joseph had it placed among Benjamin's belongings.
rows.anchor: royal scale to gauge the quantity of grain, was placed in the belonging of his brother

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanation lays out ordered details to resolve doubts that might arise about Joseph's actions.
rows.anchor: Here are some important aspects presented in order so that the doubts that may arise in the minds as a result of what Joseph did are resolved

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph did not yet reveal his identity because he wanted to see whether his brothers had changed after their crime against him.
rows.anchor: Joseph did not want to reveal his identity to his brothers. He actually wanted to investigate if his brothers had undergone some change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Having Benjamin with him, Joseph would not risk returning him to cruel brothers he suspected might repeat their foul play, since jealousy toward Benjamin persisted.
rows.anchor: he did not want to lose him at any cost. He was not prepared to undertake the danger of consigning him to his cruel brothers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph also needed to respect the just law of the land, despite the king's extraordinary favor and Joseph's broad authority.
rows.anchor: the law of the land also needed be kept in consideration. Undoubtedly because of the king’s extraordinary reverence and regard for Joseph

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In these circumstances, a just strategy required carefully worded statements that could carry a double meaning.
rows.anchor: if an effective strategy could have been adopted it had to be employing the skill of double meaning sentences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Double-meaning speech is forbidden for evil or when tainted by falsehood, but can be necessary for a just cause, especially against enemies; the Prophet also used subtle truthful examples.
rows.anchor: if it is for a just cause and also does not have any adulteration of falsehood and deception in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph called the brothers thieves for their earlier abduction and betrayal of him, not for stealing the goblet; the wording was true but could suggest a different accusation.
rows.anchor: because of what they did to Joseph (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The royal staff could regard theft of the valuable goblet as plausible after its loss was proclaimed.
rows.anchor: For this reason, its theft was not something improbable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph may have mentioned the goblet, leading the staff to assume the accusation concerned it.
rows.anchor: Joseph (sws) himself mentioned the goblet and the royal staff thought on its own that the allegation of theft

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The staff identified the goblet as missing and offered an extra camel-load to whoever found it; the speaker was probably the same person who made the proclamation.
rows.anchor: In all probability, this person was the same one who had made the proclamation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers swore they came neither to cause disorder nor steal; after hesitation, they agreed that whoever had the item in his belongings could be detained, as the penalty for wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: after a little hesitation, they replied that the person from whose belongings the stolen thing is discovered could be held back

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph searched the other brothers first to avoid suspicion, then found the goblet with Benjamin; the brothers' stated rule and confession authorized Joseph to keep him.
rows.anchor: Joseph (sws) himself started the search and started it with the other brothers instead of Benjamin so that no doubts are raised

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic term kayd means a secret plan; God inspired Joseph's plan, which protected his brother and upheld the law.
rows.anchor: This secret plan was divinely inspired in the mind of Joseph (sws). As a result of this, he was able to save his brother from danger and also uphold the law of the land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph and his staff did not lie; Benjamin temporarily faced a false charge, but knew the plan and was protected from his brothers' blame.
rows.anchor: neither Joseph (sws) nor his staff was ever implicated in any falsehood. However, for a temporary period, Benjamin was stained by face a false allegation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement about God raising some above others in rank both recognizes Joseph's status and rebukes people who claim complete knowledge from what they can observe.
rows.anchor: it is also a sarcastic remark on those who think that they have final knowledge. They think that this universe is all what they can see

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage subtly warns Quraysh not to misread the Prophet's apparent circumstances: God knows how Islam and His messenger will emerge from adversity into success.
rows.anchor: Found in this is also a subtle warning to the Quraysh who are being narrated this anecdote

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' remark hid their embarrassment and implied Joseph was their stepbrother who inherited a tendency to steal from his mother; Joseph was hurt but answered only inwardly.
rows.anchor: they wanted to give the impression that Joseph (sws) was their step brother and had inherited this tendency of stealing from his mother

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers flattered Joseph by addressing him as 'Aziz, a title reserved for Egypt's senior officials.
rows.anchor: they addressed him in a very meek way with the title of ‘Azīz, which was reserved for high officials of Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph carefully said they would not seize anyone other than the person who had their item, rather than saying anyone besides the goblet's thief.
rows.anchor: He did not say “we seize someone other than him who has stolen our goblet.” On the contrary, his words are

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reported interpretation takes 'their eminent one' as Reuben, the eldest brother.
rows.anchor: Does it refer to Reuben who was the eldest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation takes 'their eminent one' as Judas, pre-eminent among the brothers in intelligence and understanding.
rows.anchor: or to Judas who was pre-eminent among the brothers with regard to intellect and understanding

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers that the phrase mean eminence in rank and status, as in 21:63, and thus refer to Judas; if it meant eldest, another word was available.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, the word refers to eminence in rank and status as is the case with its usage in verse 63 of Sūrah al-Anbiyā’
